title: Design a Parking Garage
tagline: Model vehicles, spots, tickets and fees with clean classes, then handle two cars choosing one spot.

statement.prompt: Design the software for a **multi-storey parking garage**: drivers park, get a ticket, pay when they leave, and the garage knows what is free.
context: This is an **object-oriented (low-level) design** interview. The focus is classes, responsibilities and patterns, with a little concurrency.
You will sketch classes and method signatures. Real code is a bonus.
The garage has several floors and entrances.
given: Spots come in **small, medium and large** sizes, spread over floors.
Fees depend on how long the vehicle stayed.
Two entrances can be used at the same time.

expectations.title: Drive the conversation
expectations.body: Ask questions before drawing anything. State your assumptions out loud so they can be corrected early.

expectations.title: Use numbers
expectations.body: Turn the givens into requests per second, storage and bandwidth. Every later choice should point back to one of them.

expectations.title: Start simple, then evolve
expectations.body: Get a working version on the board first. Add caches, sharding and queues only when a number or a requirement asks for them.

expectations.title: Go deep on the hard parts
expectations.body: For this problem the hard parts are the class design, keeping pricing flexible, and avoiding two cars taking the same spot.

expectations.title: Name the trade-offs
expectations.body: Say what you chose, what you gave up, and what would make you change your mind.

expectations.title: Think about failure
expectations.body: Point out single points of failure and say what happens when a node, a cache or a whole zone goes down.

great: Derives classes from the **nouns** in the requirements.
Uses **polymorphism and Strategy** instead of if/else chains.
Spots the **race condition** on spot assignment.

concepts.def: A class should have one reason to change.
Put interchangeable algorithms (fee rules) behind one interface and pick one at runtime.
Open for extension, closed for modification: add a new class instead of editing old code.
Two actions interleave badly, such as two cars both seeing a spot as free.
Happens fully or not at all, with nothing else able to slip in between.

numbers: Fees: always **round up started hours** unless told otherwise
Pick the **smallest free spot that fits** to keep big spots available

takeaways: Start from the **nouns**: ParkingLot, Floor, Spot, Vehicle, Ticket, PricingPolicy.
Use **polymorphism** for vehicle types and the **Strategy pattern** for fees.
Make spot assignment **atomic** to prevent two cars taking one spot.
Name edge cases: lost ticket, garage full, payment failure.

tradeoffs.gain: Entrances do not block each other

extensions: Multi-garage backend with a mobile app

steps.title: What should the garage do?
steps.prompt: Clarify scope. Which features are in the **core** design?
steps.hint: What does a driver do from arriving to leaving?
steps.explain: Core: **park, unpark, vehicle types, pricing, availability display**. Say you will leave reservations for later.

notes: Core: park, unpark, vehicle types and spot sizes, pricing, free-spot display

options.text: Show whether the garage is full, with free-spot counts
options.why: Visible requirement from real garages.

options.text: Different vehicle types and spot sizes
options.why: A motorcycle should not take a truck's spot, and a truck cannot fit a small one.

options.text: Park a vehicle: find a free spot that fits and issue a ticket
options.why: The central use case.

options.text: A mobile app with online reservations and loyalty points
options.why: A separate product. Mention as a future extension.

options.text: Licence plate recognition with computer vision
options.why: Out of scope for an object model question.

options.text: Unpark: take the ticket, compute the fee, take payment, free the spot
options.why: The second half of the lifecycle.

steps.title: Find the classes
steps.prompt: Read the requirements like a detective and underline the **nouns**. Which should become classes?
steps.hint: Nouns are candidates, verbs are methods.
steps.explain: Good object design starts by **mapping nouns to classes and verbs to methods**. Merge synonyms.

notes: Classes: ParkingLot, Floor, Spot, Vehicle (+ subtypes), Ticket, PricingPolicy, Payment

options.text: PricingPolicy
options.why: The fee rules change, so isolate them.

options.text: ParkingLot
options.why: The entry point that coordinates everything.

options.text: The driver's mood
options.why: Not part of the domain.

options.text: Vehicle (Motorcycle, Car, Truck)
options.why: Types differ in the size of spot they need.

options.text: Ticket
options.why: Links a vehicle, a spot and an entry time.

options.text: The word "garage" as a second ParkingLot-like class
options.why: A synonym. Do not model the same thing twice.

options.text: Floor and Spot
options.why: A lot has floors; floors have spots.

steps.title: Model the vehicles
steps.prompt: Motorcycle, Car and Truck all need a size of spot. How do you model them?
steps.hint: Who knows what size it needs?
steps.explain: **Polymorphism over if/else.** Adding an `ElectricCar` becomes one new class.

notes: Vehicle base class with required size; subtypes Motorcycle, Car, Truck

steps.pitfall: Checking vehicle type with long if/else blocks.
steps.followup: A van takes two car spots. How would you model that?

options.text: Put the spot size inside the ParkingLot
options.why: Wrong owner of the information.

options.text: One class `Vehicle` and a string field `type` checked with if/else in every method
options.why: Every new vehicle type edits every method.

options.text: Separate unrelated classes with no shared interface
options.why: Duplicated code, and ParkingLot cannot treat them uniformly.

options.text: A base `Vehicle` with a `required_size`; `Motorcycle`, `Car`, `Truck` subclasses (or an enum) set it
options.why: The spot asks the vehicle what it needs, so no `if type == 'car'` chains.

steps.title: Trace `park()`
steps.prompt: A car arrives. Put the steps of `park(vehicle)` in order.
steps.explain: Keep each class's job small: **Lot orchestrates, Floor searches, Spot decides fit and state, Ticket records**.

notes: park(): lot -> floors find smallest fitting free spot -> atomic assign -> issue ticket -> update display

items.text: ParkingLot asks each Floor for a spot that can fit the vehicle
items.why: The lot coordinates but does not know floor internals.

items.text: Floor returns the smallest free Spot whose size fits
items.why: Smallest-fit keeps big spots free for trucks.

items.text: The Spot is marked occupied, atomically
items.why: Must not be handed to two cars.

items.text: A Ticket is created with vehicle, spot and entry time
The ticket is returned and the free-count display updates
items.why: The driver gets a ticket; the board stays accurate.

steps.title: Where do the fee rules live?
steps.prompt: Pricing may be hourly, flat per day, cheaper at night, or different per vehicle. Where do you put the logic?
steps.explain: **Strategy pattern**: `fee(ticket, exit_time)`. The same idea works for payment methods and spot-finding strategies.

notes: Pricing: PricingPolicy strategy (Hourly, Flat, ...) so rules change without touching other classes

steps.followup: How would you add a 'first 30 minutes free' rule?

options.text: Hard-coded constants in the UI
options.why: Rules must be testable and changeable.

options.text: In the Spot, because spots have prices
options.why: Spots do not know durations or vehicle types.

options.text: Inside `Ticket.calculate_fee()` with if/else for every rule
options.why: Every rule change edits a core class.

options.text: A `PricingPolicy` interface with implementations (Strategy pattern), chosen by the lot
options.why: Swap or add rules without touching ParkingLot or Ticket.

steps.title: Check the maths
steps.prompt: Hourly rate: first hour 40, then 30 for each extra started hour. A car stays **3 hours 10 minutes**. What is the fee?
steps.explain: Clarify rounding rules out loud (**started hours round up**). Unstated rules are where real systems have bugs. Put them in the `PricingPolicy`, with a unit test.

notes: Fee rule: first hour 40, then 30 per started hour (rounding up)

steps.title: Two cars, one spot
steps.prompt: Two entrances, two cars at the same time. What protects the data?
steps.hint: Make 'check free then assign' one indivisible step.
steps.explain: Hold the lock only for the **assignment**, not for the whole stay. Use a **conditional update** for simplicity.

notes: Concurrency: atomic assign (lock per floor or conditional DB update); retry on loss

steps.pitfall: Check-then-act without a lock (a race condition).

options.text: Retry with the next spot if the assignment failed
options.why: The loser simply picks another spot.

options.text: Use one global lock for the whole lot, held while the driver is parking
options.why: Serialises everyone for minutes.

options.text: Make spot assignment atomic: a lock per floor, or `UPDATE ... WHERE spot_id = ? AND free = true`
options.why: Only one caller can win.

options.text: Hope collisions are rare
options.why: Rare is not never, and a collision means two cars in one spot.

options.text: Keep the state in one place (database or single service) rather than in each entrance's memory
options.why: Two entrances with separate copies disagree.

steps.title: Edge cases
steps.prompt: Which edge cases would you mention?
steps.explain: Naming 3 to 4 edge cases shows **engineering maturity**.

notes: Edge cases: lost ticket, garage full, payment failure, oversize vehicle

options.text: Assume nothing ever goes wrong
options.why: Interviewers specifically look for this thinking.

options.text: Garage full: reject at the entrance and show the board
options.why: Fail fast, do not queue cars in the street.

options.text: Payment fails: keep the vehicle's spot and allow a retry
options.why: Never free the spot before payment succeeds.

options.text: Lost ticket: charge a flat maximum fee, verify by plate
options.why: A real-world rule every garage has.

options.text: Vehicle too big for any spot: reject with a clear message
options.why: Handle the impossible case explicitly.

steps.title: A chain of 500 garages
steps.prompt: Now it is a company with 500 garages and a mobile app showing free spots. What changes?
steps.hint: What stays the same, what moves out?
steps.explain: Good object design survives scale: **persist the same entities** (`Spot`, `Ticket`) in a database, expose `POST /park` and `POST /unpark`, and read counts from a cache or a counter table.

notes: Scaling out: persist Spot and Ticket in a database, expose park/unpark APIs, cache free counts

options.text: Turn `ParkingLot` into a service with a database for spot and ticket state, and cache the free count per floor
options.why: State leaves the process; the object model stays the same.

options.text: Remove floors from the model
options.why: Floors are still a real concept.

options.text: Rewrite all classes
options.why: A good model survives a change of scale. Only storage and APIs change.

options.text: Keep everything in memory on each garage's PC and sync by email
options.why: No shared view, no durability.

steps.title: Defend your design
steps.prompt: In two or three sentences: what design principles guided you, and where might they cost you?
steps.explain: In OOD interviews, **name the pattern and the reason**, not just the pattern.

notes: Trade-offs: flexibility (patterns) vs simplicity; narrow locks

steps.model: I used **single responsibility** (each class does one job), **polymorphism** for vehicles, and the **Strategy pattern** for pricing so rules change without editing core classes. The cost is **more classes and indirection** than a quick script. I kept locking narrow, only around spot assignment, to avoid slowing down entrances. If requirements stayed this small I would simplify, but the extension points (new vehicle types, new fee rules) are where real garages change.
